what_this_tests: EBS is single-AZ block storage. EFS is multi-AZ shared file storage.
Instance store is temporary and host-attached. EBS persists.
EFS serves Linux over NFS. FSx for Windows serves SMB with Active Directory.

signal_words.phrase: persistent block storage attached to an EC2 instance
shared NFS/POSIX file system across many instances and AZs
Windows SMB share with Active Directory and NTFS ACLs
signal_words.points_to: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server

signal_words.phrase: temporary buffers, caches, or scratch data
one volume shared by a cluster inside a single AZ

core_services.name: Amazon EBS
core_services.job: Block storage volumes attached to EC2 instances, plus point-in-time snapshots.
core_services.choose_when: A database or app on EC2 needs low-latency persistent storage that survives reboots.
core_services.avoid_when: Instances in different AZs must share one file system. Use EFS. An EBS volume lives in one AZ.
core_services.trap_words: multi-AZ shared file system, object storage
core_services.aws_official_description: Amazon EBS provides scalable, high-performance block storage for EC2 instances. An attached volume is used like a local hard drive.
verified_claims: io2 Block Express: 99.999% durability, 0.001% annual failure rate. Other types: 99.8%-99.9%.
Volume data is replicated across multiple servers within a single Availability Zone.
Multi-Attach: io1/io2 only, up to 16 Nitro instances, same AZ, never a boot volume.

core_services.name: Amazon EFS
core_services.job: Serverless elastic NFS file storage. Grows and shrinks automatically as files change.
core_services.choose_when: Many Linux EC2, ECS, EKS, Fargate, or Lambda clients share one POSIX file tree across AZs.
core_services.avoid_when: The workload runs on Windows EC2 instances. AWS does not support that. Use FSx for Windows.
core_services.trap_words: Windows SMB, single-instance block device
core_services.aws_official_description: Amazon EFS provides serverless, fully elastic file storage. It scales on demand to petabytes without provisioning capacity or disrupting applications.
verified_claims: Supports NFSv4.1 and NFSv4.0, plus POSIX permissions.
Regional file systems span multiple AZs. One Zone file systems stay in a single AZ.
AWS states EFS with Microsoft Windows-based EC2 instances is not supported.

core_services.name: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
core_services.job: Managed Windows file servers on a native Windows file system, over SMB.
core_services.choose_when: Windows apps need NTFS ACLs and Active Directory authentication.
core_services.avoid_when: The workload is Linux and expects NFS/POSIX. Use EFS.
core_services.trap_words: Linux NFS, POSIX permissions
core_services.aws_official_description: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server provides fully managed Microsoft Windows file servers backed by a native Windows file system, accessed over the SMB protocol.
verified_claims: Supports SMB 2.0 through 3.1.1. Users authenticate with Microsoft Active Directory.
Multi-AZ deployments maintain a standby file server in a second AZ. Single-AZ does not.
Storage capacity, SSD IOPS, and throughput capacity are provisioned independently.

core_services.name: EC2 instance store
core_services.job: Temporary block storage on disks physically attached to the host.
core_services.choose_when: You need fast local storage for buffers, caches, or regenerable scratch data.
core_services.avoid_when: Data must survive a stop, hibernate, or terminate. Every block is cryptographically erased.
core_services.trap_words: persistent, durable, snapshot backups
core_services.aws_official_description: An instance store provides temporary block-level storage from disks physically attached to the host computer. It suits frequently changing data such as buffers, caches, and scratch data.
verified_claims: Data persists across a reboot. It does not persist across stop, hibernate, or terminate.
Instance store volumes attach only at launch. They cannot be detached or moved.
No additional charge. Included in the instance usage cost.

comparisons: EBS vs EFS: an EBS volume is single-AZ and normally one instance (Multi-Attach allows 16 Nitro instances in one AZ, io1/io2). A Regional EFS file system spans multiple AZs with massively parallel access.
EFS vs FSx for Windows: EFS is NFSv4 with POSIX permissions and unsupported on Windows EC2. FSx for Windows is SMB 2.0-3.1.1 with NTFS ACLs and Active Directory.
EBS vs instance store: EBS survives stops and snapshots to S3. Instance store survives only reboots.
exam_moves: Servers in multiple AZs writing the same directory means EFS, not EBS.
High-IOPS database on EC2 with the highest durability means io2 / io2 Block Express (99.999%).
'Data is lost when the instance stops' identifies the instance store.
'NTFS permissions', 'SMB share', or 'joins Active Directory' rules out EFS and selects FSx for Windows.

what_this_tests: Matching storage class to access pattern, then automating with S3 Lifecycle.
Object Lock enforces WORM via retention periods and legal holds.
Versioning recovers accidental overwrites and deletes.
Glacier minimum durations: 90, 90, 180 days. Retrieval: milliseconds, minutes-hours, hours.

signal_words.phrase: unknown, changing, or unpredictable access patterns
accessed less than once a year, hours to retrieve, cheapest
archive that still needs millisecond retrieval
recover from accidental overwrite or deletion
cannot be deleted even by the root user
transition or expire objects after N days

core_services.name: S3 storage classes
core_services.job: Per-object tiers tuned to access pattern: Standard, Intelligent-Tiering, Standard-IA, One Zone-IA, Express One Zone, three Glacier classes.
core_services.choose_when: You want cheaper storage for infrequent or rare access without leaving S3.
core_services.avoid_when: You need a block device (EBS) or a POSIX file system (EFS).
core_services.trap_words: block storage, EBS replacement, file system mount
core_services.aws_official_description: Every S3 object has a storage class. S3 Standard is the default. Choosing the class designed for your use case optimizes storage cost, performance, and availability.
verified_claims: All classes are designed for 99.999999999% durability except Reduced Redundancy Storage at 99.99%.
Minimum durations: 30 days Standard-IA and One Zone-IA; 90 days Glacier Instant and Flexible; 180 days Deep Archive.
Glacier Instant Retrieval is millisecond access. Flexible Retrieval is minutes to hours. Deep Archive is hours. Both latter require a restore.

core_services.name: S3 Lifecycle configuration
core_services.job: Rules that transition objects to cheaper classes or expire them on a schedule.
core_services.choose_when: Logs or backups must move to IA or Glacier after N days and be deleted at end of retention.
core_services.avoid_when: An action must fire the instant an object lands. Use S3 Event Notifications.
core_services.trap_words: instant trigger, event-driven processing
core_services.aws_official_description: An S3 Lifecycle configuration is a set of rules defining actions S3 applies to a group of objects. Transition actions move objects to another storage class. Expiration actions delete them.
verified_claims: Rules apply to existing objects as well as objects added later.
A bucket policy cannot block deletions or transitions performed by a Lifecycle rule.
AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload expires orphaned multipart parts after N days.

core_services.name: S3 Object Lock
core_services.job: WORM storage. Blocks delete and overwrite of an object version for a fixed period or indefinitely.
core_services.choose_when: Regulation demands immutability. Compliance mode blocks even the account root user.
core_services.avoid_when: You only need rollback of accidental changes. Versioning is enough.
core_services.trap_words: accidental deletion only, simple rollback
core_services.aws_official_description: S3 Object Lock prevents objects from being deleted or overwritten for a fixed time or indefinitely, using a write-once-read-many (WORM) model, to help meet regulatory WORM requirements.
verified_claims: Object Lock works only in buckets with S3 Versioning enabled.
Compliance mode: no user, including the root user, can overwrite or delete; retention cannot be shortened.
Governance mode can be overridden with the s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission.
Assessed by Cohasset Associates for SEC 17a-4, CFTC, and FINRA environments.

core_services.name: S3 Versioning
core_services.job: Keeps multiple variants of an object in one bucket so any version can be restored.
core_services.choose_when: You need simple recovery after an accidental overwrite or delete.
core_services.avoid_when: Regulation requires immutability for a defined period. Add Object Lock.
core_services.trap_words: regulatory WORM, legal hold, immutable retention
core_services.aws_official_description: S3 Versioning keeps multiple variants of an object in the same bucket. You can preserve, retrieve, and restore every version of every object.
verified_claims: Versioning is off by default. Once enabled, a bucket can only be suspended, never returned to unversioned.
A delete in a versioned bucket inserts a delete marker rather than removing the object.
Each version is a full object, not a diff. Three versions bill as three objects.

core_services.name: S3 Multipart Upload
core_services.job: Uploads one object as independent parts, then assembles them. Failed parts retry alone.
core_services.choose_when: Uploading large objects. AWS recommends multipart at 100 MB or larger.
core_services.avoid_when: Objects are small. A single PutObject is simpler.
core_services.trap_words: small files, download acceleration
core_services.aws_official_description: Multipart upload uploads a single object as a set of parts. Parts upload independently and in any order. A failed part can be retransmitted without affecting the others.
verified_claims: AWS best practice: use multipart upload for objects 100 MB or larger.
Part numbers range from 1 to 10,000.
You are billed for uploaded parts until you complete or stop the upload.

core_services.name: S3 Reduced Redundancy Storage (RRS)
core_services.job: Legacy class for noncritical, reproducible data with less redundancy than S3 Standard.
core_services.choose_when: Rarely. AWS recommends against it; S3 Standard is more cost-effective. Use One Zone-IA for recreatable data.
core_services.avoid_when: Data is unique, critical, or cannot be regenerated.
core_services.trap_words: critical data, highly durable, cheapest archive
core_services.aws_official_description: Reduced Redundancy Storage is designed for noncritical, reproducible data stored with less redundancy than S3 Standard. AWS recommends not using this storage class.
verified_claims: Designed for 99.99% durability, an average annual expected loss of 0.01% of objects.
Requests for a lost RRS object return a 405 error.
AWS documentation explicitly recommends not using RRS.

comparisons: Standard vs Intelligent-Tiering: use Standard for known frequent access. Intelligent-Tiering moves objects automatically, charges a per-object monitoring fee, and has no retrieval fees. Objects under 128 KB are not monitored.

Versioning vs Object Lock: Versioning preserves old versions but a privileged user can still delete them. Object Lock blocks delete and overwrite for a retention period or legal hold, and requires versioning.

Standard-IA vs One Zone-IA: both 11 nines durability, 30-day minimum, 128 KB minimum billable size. Standard-IA spans 3+ AZs at 99.9% availability. One Zone-IA is one AZ at 99.5%, cheaper, and lost if that AZ is lost.
Glacier classes: Instant Retrieval is milliseconds, 90-day minimum. Flexible Retrieval is minutes to hours, 90-day minimum. Deep Archive is hours, 180-day minimum.
exam_moves: 'Not deletable by anyone including root, for N years' means Object Lock compliance mode plus versioning.
Hot for 30 days then cold means a Lifecycle rule to Standard-IA or Glacier, with an expiration action.
Millisecond archive access means Glacier Instant Retrieval, not Flexible Retrieval.
A 50 GB upload over a spotty link means S3 Multipart Upload.
'Unknown access patterns' plus 'no retrieval fees' means Intelligent-Tiering.

what_this_tests: Online transfer (DataSync) versus offline physical transfer (Snow Family).
EBS snapshots are incremental, stored in S3, replicated across AZs in the Region.
Storage Gateway gives on-premises apps file, block, or tape access to AWS storage.
AWS Backup centralizes policies across services and accounts. Vault Lock adds WORM.

signal_words.phrase: internet transfer would take months
sync on-premises files to S3, EFS, or FSx over the network
on-premises servers need NFS, SMB, or iSCSI backed by AWS
incremental point-in-time block backups
centralized policy-based backup across services and accounts
backups nobody can delete or shorten

core_services.name: AWS Backup
core_services.job: Centralizes and automates backups across AWS services with plans, tags, lifecycle, and cross-Region/account copies.
core_services.choose_when: One policy must cover EC2/EBS, RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB, EFS, FSx, S3, and Storage Gateway volumes.
core_services.avoid_when: You need a single ad hoc snapshot, or the resource type is unsupported.
core_services.trap_words: manual one-off snapshot, single service only
core_services.aws_official_description: AWS Backup is a fully managed service that centralizes and automates data protection across AWS services, in the cloud and on premises. You configure backup policies and monitor activity in one place.
verified_claims: Supported resources include EC2 (EBS-backed), EBS, S3, RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB, EFS, FSx, DocumentDB, Neptune, Redshift, and Storage Gateway volumes.
AWS Backup Vault Lock enforces WORM. Nobody, including you, can delete backups or alter retention.
Backups copy across Regions and across accounts in an AWS Organizations structure, on demand or on schedule.

core_services.name: AWS DataSync
core_services.job: Online, high-speed transfer of file and object data to, from, and between AWS storage services.
core_services.choose_when: Bandwidth is adequate and you need scheduled or repeated syncs from NFS, SMB, HDFS, or object storage.
core_services.avoid_when: Bandwidth cannot move the data set in the required window. Use an offline transfer.
core_services.trap_words: offline shipping, physical appliance
core_services.aws_official_description: AWS DataSync is a secure, reliable, high-speed file transfer service that transfers file or object data to, from, and between AWS storage services.
verified_claims: Sources include on-premises NFS, SMB, HDFS, and object storage. Destinations include S3, EFS, and FSx for Windows, Lustre, OpenZFS, and NetApp ONTAP.
Provides end-to-end encryption and data integrity validation, and supports VPC endpoints to avoid the public internet.
Can move cold data directly into S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive.

core_services.name: AWS Snowball Edge
core_services.job: Ruggedized physical device with storage and compute. Ships data to S3 without using the internet.
core_services.choose_when: Classic exam scenario: huge data set, internet transfer would take months.
core_services.avoid_when: The network can carry the transfer. Note AWS closed Snowball Edge to new customers and points them to DataSync, AWS Data Transfer Terminal, partners, or Outposts.
core_services.trap_words: continuous sync, online transfer, low-latency hybrid access
core_services.aws_official_description: Snowball Edge is a device with on-board storage and compute power. It processes data locally, runs edge-computing workloads, and transfers data to or from the AWS Cloud faster than the internet.
verified_claims: Configurations: Storage Optimized 210 TB and Compute Optimized. Network adapters up to 100 Gbit/s. Encryption enforced.
AWS states Snowball Edge is no longer available to new customers, and support ends December 31, 2026 in all commercial Regions.
Supports NFSv3, NFSv4, NFSv4.1, and S3 over HTTP/HTTPS. Devices cluster across 3 to 16 nodes.

core_services.name: Amazon EBS snapshots
core_services.job: Incremental point-in-time backups of EBS volumes, stored in AWS-managed S3 buckets.
core_services.choose_when: You must back up a volume, restore it into another AZ, or build an AMI.
core_services.avoid_when: You need file-level backup of a shared file system. Use AWS Backup with EFS or FSx.
core_services.trap_words: file-level restore, synchronous replication
core_services.aws_official_description: An Amazon EBS snapshot is a point-in-time copy of a volume. Snapshots are incremental: only blocks changed since the most recent snapshot are saved.
verified_claims: Snapshots live in S3 buckets you cannot reach through the S3 console or API.
Snapshot data replicates across all AZs in the Region, so volumes restore into any AZ there.
Deleting a snapshot removes only blocks it exclusively references. Other snapshots stay valid.

core_services.name: AWS Storage Gateway
core_services.job: On-premises appliance giving local apps file, block, or tape access to AWS storage with a local cache.
core_services.choose_when: Servers must keep using NFS/SMB shares, iSCSI volumes, or virtual tape while data lives in S3.
core_services.avoid_when: It is a one-time bulk migration with no ongoing hybrid access. Use DataSync or offline transfer.
core_services.trap_words: one-time migration, offline shipping
core_services.aws_official_description: Amazon S3 File Gateway gives a file interface into Amazon S3. You store and retrieve S3 objects using NFS and SMB, with low-latency access through transparent local caching.
verified_claims: Gateway types: S3 File Gateway, FSx File Gateway, Volume Gateway, Tape Gateway.
S3 File Gateway supports NFS v3 and v4.1 and SMB v2 and v3. Deploys on ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM, hardware appliance, or EC2.
Volume Gateway cached volumes keep primary data in S3 with a local cache. Stored volumes keep all data local and snapshot it to S3.

comparisons: DataSync vs Storage Gateway: DataSync copies or syncs data into AWS over the network. Storage Gateway leaves apps on premises and gives them NFS/SMB, iSCSI, or tape access to AWS-backed storage.
Offline vs online: pick offline transfer when bandwidth cannot meet the deadline; pick DataSync when it can. AWS has closed Snowball Edge to new customers and ends support December 31, 2026.
S3 File Gateway vs Volume Gateway: File Gateway exposes S3 objects as NFS/SMB files. Volume Gateway exposes iSCSI block volumes backed by point-in-time snapshots.
EBS snapshots vs AWS Backup: snapshots are the per-volume mechanism. AWS Backup adds plans, tag assignment, retention lifecycle, cross-Region and cross-account copy, Vault Lock, and Audit Manager.
exam_moves: Poor connectivity plus a very large data set means offline transfer (Snow Family in classic wording; DataSync or Data Transfer Terminal under current AWS guidance).
EBS snapshot data replicates across all AZs in the Region, so a snapshot restores a volume into another AZ.
Deleting an old EBS snapshot never breaks newer snapshots.
Daily schedule with 30-day retention across EBS, RDS, and DynamoDB means AWS Backup.
'Backup retention cannot be shortened by anyone' means AWS Backup Vault Lock.

iSCSI block volumes, primary data in S3, local cache
keep entire dataset on-premises, back up as EBS snapshots

core_services.name: AWS Storage Gateway File Gateway
core_services.job: Serves NFS/SMB shares on-premises. Stores each file as an S3 object.
core_services.choose_when: Servers must write to a local SMB or NFS share, readable afterward as native S3 objects.
core_services.avoid_when: The application needs iSCSI block devices. Use Volume Gateway.
core_services.trap_words: block storage, local iSCSI
core_services.aws_official_description: Amazon S3 File Gateway provides a file interface into Amazon S3, combining a service and a virtual software appliance. You store and retrieve objects in Amazon S3 using NFS and SMB.
verified_claims: Supports NFS version 3 and 4.1, and SMB version 2 and 3.
Stored objects support S3 lifecycle policies, cross-Region replication, and versioning.
Deploys as a VM on VMware ESXi, Hyper-V, or Linux KVM, as a hardware appliance, or as an EC2 AMI.

core_services.name: AWS Storage Gateway Volume Gateway (cached)
core_services.job: Serves iSCSI volumes. S3 holds primary data; hot blocks stay in a local cache.
core_services.choose_when: You want to shrink on-premises SAN capacity but keep hot blocks low-latency.
core_services.avoid_when: The whole dataset needs local low-latency access. Use stored volumes.
core_services.trap_words: file storage, NFS, SMB
core_services.aws_official_description: Cached volumes use Amazon S3 as primary data storage while retaining frequently accessed data locally in the Storage Gateway.
verified_claims: Cached volumes range from 1 GiB to 32 TiB. Each gateway supports 32 volumes, 1,024 TiB (1 PiB) total.
Local disks are allocated as cache storage and upload buffer.
Snapshots are incremental and stored in Amazon S3 as EBS snapshots.

core_services.name: AWS Storage Gateway Volume Gateway (stored)
core_services.job: Serves iSCSI volumes whose primary data stays on-premises. Backs up async as EBS snapshots.
core_services.choose_when: The full dataset must stay local, with durable offsite backup in AWS.
core_services.avoid_when: The goal is freeing local disk by making the cloud primary. Use cached volumes.
core_services.trap_words: cloud-primary storage, saving local disk space
core_services.aws_official_description: Stored volumes keep primary data locally while asynchronously backing it up to AWS. They give on-premises applications low-latency access to their entire datasets.
verified_claims: Stored volumes range from 1 GiB to 16 TiB. Each gateway supports 32 volumes, 512 TiB (0.5 PiB) total.
Data lives on on-premises hardware and is backed up to S3 as EBS snapshots.
A snapshot can restore the gateway volume or seed a new EBS volume for EC2.

comparisons: File Gateway vs Volume Gateway: File Gateway writes native S3 objects readable by the S3 API. Volume Gateway writes EBS snapshots, not S3-API-accessible.
Cached vs stored: Cached makes S3 primary, 32 TiB per volume, hot data local. Stored keeps everything local, 16 TiB per volume, snapshots only in AWS.
exam_moves: SMB or NFS share on-premises, files must become S3 objects: S3 File Gateway.
Local SAN is full and iSCSI volumes should be cloud-backed with a hot cache: cached volumes.
Entire dataset must stay local but needs offsite DR: stored volumes.

what_this_tests: RDS engines versus Aurora for a managed relational workload.
Multi-AZ is availability. Read replicas are read scaling. Questions blur the two.
RDS Proxy for connection exhaustion. DMS for near-zero-downtime migration.

signal_words.phrase: managed relational database, AWS patches and backs up
MySQL/PostgreSQL-compatible, storage auto-grows
automatic failover to a synchronous standby
offload read-heavy reporting queries
Lambda functions exhausting DB connections
migrate while the source stays operational

core_services.name: Amazon RDS
core_services.job: Runs managed relational databases. AWS owns OS, patching, backups, and failover.
core_services.choose_when: You want SQL with ACID transactions and no server administration.
core_services.avoid_when: You need OS-level or SSH access. Run the database on EC2 instead.
core_services.trap_words: NoSQL, OS-level access, key-value store
core_services.aws_official_description: Amazon RDS is a web service that makes it easier to set up, operate, and scale a relational database in the AWS Cloud. It provides resizable capacity and manages common database administration tasks.
verified_claims: RDS supports six engines: IBM Db2, MariaDB, Microsoft SQL Server, MySQL, Oracle Database, PostgreSQL.
AWS owns scaling, HA, backups, DB patching, DB install, OS patching, and OS install. On EC2 the customer owns all of those.
Storage is General Purpose SSD or Provisioned IOPS SSD. Magnetic is deprecated for new instances.

core_services.name: Amazon Aurora
core_services.job: MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible engine on a shared distributed storage volume.
core_services.choose_when: You need higher throughput than stock MySQL/PostgreSQL, auto-growing storage, or fast replica failover.
core_services.avoid_when: The workload runs Oracle, SQL Server, MariaDB, or Db2. Aurora supports none of them.
core_services.trap_words: Oracle, SQL Server, NoSQL
core_services.aws_official_description: Amazon Aurora is a fully managed relational database engine compatible with MySQL and PostgreSQL. It delivers up to 6x the throughput of stock PostgreSQL and up to 6x the throughput of stock MySQL on similar hardware.
verified_claims: The cluster volume holds copies of the data across three Availability Zones in one Region.
Cluster volumes grow automatically to a maximum of 256 TiB.
An Aurora DB cluster supports up to 15 Aurora Replicas. Aurora promotes one automatically if the writer fails.

core_services.name: RDS Multi-AZ
core_services.job: Maintains a synchronous standby replica in another AZ, with automatic failover.
core_services.choose_when: You need availability, data redundancy, or failover for production.
core_services.avoid_when: You need read scaling. The standby serves no reads.
core_services.trap_words: scaling reads, performance improvement
core_services.aws_official_description: In a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, Amazon RDS automatically provisions and maintains a synchronous standby replica in a different Availability Zone, providing data redundancy and minimizing latency spikes during system backups.
verified_claims: AWS states Multi-AZ is not a scaling solution for read-only scenarios; the standby cannot serve read traffic.
MariaDB, MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, and RDS Custom for SQL Server use Amazon failover technology. SQL Server uses Database Mirroring or Always On Availability Groups.
A Multi-AZ DB cluster has one writer and two readers across three AZs. All three serve reads.

core_services.name: RDS Read Replicas
core_services.job: Creates asynchronous read-only copies of a DB instance to absorb read traffic.
core_services.choose_when: Reporting, BI, or analytics reads are overloading the primary.
core_services.avoid_when: You need automatic failover. Replicas are async and must be promoted manually.
core_services.trap_words: automatic failover, synchronous replication
core_services.aws_official_description: A read replica is a read-only copy of a DB instance. Routing queries to it reduces load on the primary and scales out beyond the capacity of a single DB instance for read-heavy workloads.
verified_claims: RDS copies updates to the replica asynchronously using the engine's built-in replication.
A replica can be promoted to a standalone instance. AWS lists this as a DR option.
Replicas can live in a different Region. RDS builds a secure channel between them.
RDS does not autoscale read replicas. You create and delete them manually.

core_services.name: RDS Proxy
core_services.job: Pools and shares database connections. Preserves application connections during failover.
core_services.choose_when: Lambda or other short-lived clients oversubscribe the database with connections.
core_services.avoid_when: You want query caching or read scaling. A proxy attaches only to the writer.
core_services.trap_words: caching queries, reading data faster
core_services.aws_official_description: Amazon RDS Proxy lets applications pool and share database connections to improve scalability. It makes applications more resilient to database failures by automatically connecting to a standby DB instance while preserving application connections.
verified_claims: The proxy can enforce IAM authentication for clients and connect using IAM auth or AWS Secrets Manager credentials.
Each account is limited to 20 proxies. Each proxy supports up to 200 Secrets Manager secrets.
In replication configurations, a proxy attaches only to the writer DB instance, never a read replica.

core_services.name: AWS DMS
core_services.job: Migrates relational, warehouse, and NoSQL data stores. One-time load or ongoing replication.
core_services.choose_when: A source database must stay online during migration, including a change of engine.
core_services.avoid_when: You are moving file shares (DataSync) or whole servers (Application Migration Service).
core_services.trap_words: file migration, VM migration
core_services.aws_official_description: AWS DMS migrates relational databases, data warehouses, NoSQL databases, and other data stores. You can perform one-time migrations or replicate ongoing changes to keep sources and targets in sync.
verified_claims: DMS supports fully heterogeneous migrations. DMS Schema Conversion or AWS SCT converts the source schema.
If the primary replication server fails, a backup replication server takes over with little or no interruption.
Data at rest is encrypted with AWS KMS. SSL encrypts data in flight.

comparisons: Multi-AZ vs read replicas: the Multi-AZ standby is synchronous and serves no reads. Read replicas are async, scale reads, and need manual promotion.
RDS vs Aurora: RDS runs six engines on per-instance EBS. Aurora is MySQL/PostgreSQL-only. It replicates across three AZs, grows to 256 TiB, supports 15 replicas, and reaches 6x stock throughput.
RDS vs EC2: RDS gives AWS the OS, patching, backups, HA, and scaling. Choose EC2 only for OS access or an unsupported engine.
exam_moves: Reporting slows the primary: add a read replica and point reporting at it.
High availability or automatic failover required: enable Multi-AZ. The standby is not readable.
Thousands of Lambda functions exhaust connections: put RDS Proxy in front.
Source must stay online and the engine changes: DMS plus DMS Schema Conversion or AWS SCT.

what_this_tests: DynamoDB for serverless key-value and document workloads at single-digit millisecond latency.
Built-in resilience: three-AZ replication, global tables, PITR, on-demand capacity.
The real DynamoDB limit is no JOIN, not missing transactions.

signal_words.phrase: single-digit millisecond NoSQL at any scale
multi-Region multi-active, 99.999% availability
restore to any second in the last 35 days
unpredictable traffic, pay per request, scales to zero

core_services.name: Amazon DynamoDB
core_services.job: Serverless distributed NoSQL database. Key-value and document models, single-digit millisecond latency.
core_services.choose_when: You need shopping carts, session state, game state, or leaderboards at scale with no servers.
core_services.avoid_when: The model needs SQL JOINs or a normalized relational schema. Use RDS or Aurora.
core_services.trap_words: SQL joins, relational schema, normalized data
core_services.aws_official_description: Amazon DynamoDB is a serverless, fully managed, distributed NoSQL database with single-digit millisecond performance at any scale. It supports both key-value and document data models.
verified_claims: DynamoDB replicates data across three Availability Zones by default with a 99.99% availability SLA. Global tables raise it to 99.999%.
DynamoDB provides native server-side ACID transactions across items and tables in one request, plus strong read consistency.
Point-in-time recovery restores a table to any second in the last 35 days. The window is configurable from 1 to 35 days.
DynamoDB has no JOIN operator. AWS recommends denormalizing the data model.

comparisons: DynamoDB vs RDS: DynamoDB is serverless NoSQL with no JOIN, built for denormalized models and horizontal scale. RDS is relational with joins, schemas, and replica-based read scaling.

ElastiCache Valkey/Redis OSS vs Memcached: Valkey and Redis OSS give replication, automatic failover, sorted sets, pub/sub, backup and restore. Memcached is multi-threaded and simple, with none of those.
DAX vs ElastiCache: DAX caches only DynamoDB and serves eventually consistent reads. ElastiCache caches anything, including RDS results and session state.
exam_moves: Shopping cart or session state at scale with no server management: DynamoDB.
An answer claiming DynamoDB lacks transactions is a distractor. It has ACID transactions across tables.
Local reads and writes in several Regions with no failover step: DynamoDB global tables.

what_this_tests: DAX when the backing store is DynamoDB and reads can be eventually consistent.
Valkey/Redis OSS for failover and complex types. Memcached for the simplest object cache.
What caching does not fix: write-heavy workloads and strongly consistent reads.

signal_words.phrase: microsecond DynamoDB reads with no application rewrite
cache RDS results, session state, or leaderboards
simplest cache, large multi-core nodes, scale out and in
no capacity planning, cache ready in under a minute

core_services.name: DAX (DynamoDB Accelerator)
core_services.job: DynamoDB-compatible in-memory cache. Cuts eventually consistent reads from milliseconds to microseconds.
core_services.choose_when: A DynamoDB table has repeated reads of the same items or a hot key.
core_services.avoid_when: You need strongly consistent reads, the workload is write-heavy, or the data is not in DynamoDB.
core_services.trap_words: RDS caching, strongly consistent reads, write-heavy
core_services.aws_official_description: DAX is a DynamoDB-compatible caching service that reduces the response times of eventually consistent read workloads by an order of magnitude, from single-digit milliseconds to microseconds.
verified_claims: DAX delivers up to 10x performance improvement, milliseconds to microseconds, at millions of requests per second.
DAX is API-compatible with DynamoDB and needs only minimal functional changes.
AWS states DAX is not ideal for strongly consistent reads or write-intensive workloads. It performs best above a 90% cache hit rate.

core_services.name: Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey / Redis OSS
core_services.job: Managed in-memory data store with complex data types, replication, and automatic failover.
core_services.choose_when: You need RDS query caching, sorted-set leaderboards, session state, pub/sub, or failover.
core_services.avoid_when: You only need a simple object cache on large multi-core nodes. Use Memcached.
core_services.trap_words: simple caching, no failover required, multi-threaded
core_services.aws_official_description: Amazon ElastiCache supports the Valkey, Memcached, and Redis OSS engines. Choose Valkey or Redis OSS for complex data types, replication, automatic failover, pub/sub, sorted sets, and backup and restore.
verified_claims: Valkey and Redis OSS clusters support replication, pub/sub, sorted sets, geospatial indexing, and backup and restore.
Automatic failover is optional with cluster mode disabled and required with cluster mode enabled.
Valkey and Redis OSS clusters are not multi-threaded. Memcached is.
ElastiCache Serverless supports Valkey 7.2+, Memcached 1.6.22+, and Redis OSS 7.1, and creates a cache in under a minute.

core_services.name: Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached
core_services.job: Simplest multi-threaded in-memory object cache. Scales out and in by adding or removing nodes.
core_services.choose_when: You want the simplest model, large multi-core nodes, and plain object caching.
core_services.avoid_when: You need replication, automatic failover, sorted sets, or pub/sub. Use Valkey or Redis OSS.
core_services.trap_words: high availability, automatic failover, complex data types
core_services.aws_official_description: Choose Memcached when you need the simplest model possible, large nodes with multiple cores or threads, the ability to scale out and in as demand changes, and object caching.
verified_claims: AWS's engine table lists Memcached as multi-threaded, with no replication, no automatic failover, no pub/sub, and no sorted sets.
Memcached supports data partitioning and node type upgrades from engine version 1.5 and later.
Backup and restore for Memcached applies to serverless caches only, not node-based clusters.

comparisons: DAX vs ElastiCache: DAX is DynamoDB-only, API-compatible, up to 10x faster, eventually consistent. ElastiCache is engine-agnostic and you populate it yourself.
Valkey/Redis OSS vs Memcached: the first adds replication, failover, complex types, pub/sub, and backups. Memcached adds multi-threading and partitioning only.
ElastiCache Serverless vs node-based: serverless removes capacity planning and builds a cache in under a minute. Node-based controls node type, count, AZ placement, cluster mode, and patch timing.
exam_moves: DynamoDB needs microsecond reads with no rewrite: DAX, but only if eventual consistency is acceptable.
Cache relational results or session state with Multi-AZ failover: ElastiCache for Valkey or Redis OSS.
Simple horizontally scalable object cache, failover not required: ElastiCache for Memcached.

core_services.name: Amazon OpenSearch Service
core_services.job: Deploys, operates, and scales OpenSearch clusters, called domains, for search and analytics.
core_services.choose_when: You need catalog full-text search, or log analytics, SIEM, application monitoring, or clickstream analysis.
core_services.avoid_when: You need a transactional system of record (RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB) or one-off SQL over S3 (Athena).
core_services.trap_words: primary database, system of record, relational transactions
core_services.aws_official_description: Amazon OpenSearch Service is a managed service for deploying, operating, and scaling OpenSearch clusters in the AWS Cloud. OpenSearch is an open-source search and analytics engine for log analytics, real-time application monitoring, and clickstream analysis.
verified_claims: A domain is synonymous with a cluster. The service detects and replaces failed nodes automatically.
OpenSearch Service supports up to 1,002 data nodes and 25 PB of attached storage, plus UltraWarm and cold storage.
It supports OpenSearch and legacy Elasticsearch OSS up to 7.10, the final open source version.
Nodes can be allocated across two or three Availability Zones (Multi-AZ).

comparisons: OpenSearch Service vs Athena: OpenSearch runs an indexed cluster billed by the hour, with relevance ranking and dashboards. Athena is serverless, queries S3 in place with SQL, and bills per query.
OpenSearch vs a database: OpenSearch is an index beside the system of record. RDS, Aurora, and DynamoDB hold the durable data and feed it.
Firehose vs Kinesis Data Streams into OpenSearch: Firehose delivers with no application to write. Data Streams requires a consumer you build.
exam_moves: Full-text search over a product catalog: OpenSearch Service, not a SQL LIKE query.
Index, search, and dashboard logs in near real time: OpenSearch Service, usually fed by Amazon Data Firehose.
Occasional SQL over data already in S3, no infrastructure: Athena, not an OpenSearch domain.

serverless data catalog and ETL
ad-hoc SQL directly on S3, no infrastructure

deliver streaming data to S3 with no code

core_services.name: Amazon Redshift
core_services.job: Petabyte-scale data warehouse. Columnar storage, leader node plus parallel compute slices.
core_services.choose_when: Complex BI and SQL analytics over huge historical datasets.
core_services.avoid_when: High-throughput OLTP for a live app. Use RDS or Aurora.
core_services.trap_words: OLTP, live application database, single-row updates
core_services.aws_official_description: Amazon Redshift is a fully managed, petabyte-scale data warehouse service in the cloud. Redshift Serverless provisions resources automatically and scales capacity without configuring a provisioned data warehouse.
verified_claims: Redshift is a fully managed, petabyte-scale data warehouse; runs provisioned or serverless.
A leader node builds execution plans; compute nodes split into slices that run in parallel.
Redshift uses columnar storage with a 1 MB block size. AWS states row storage is optimal for OLTP.

core_services.name: Amazon Athena
core_services.job: Runs standard SQL directly on S3 data. Serverless; pay per query.
core_services.choose_when: Query VPC Flow Logs, CloudTrail, or app logs in S3 without loading them anywhere.
core_services.avoid_when: Continuous high-concurrency BI reporting. Use Redshift.
core_services.trap_words: dedicated data warehouse, continuous BI, provisioned cluster
core_services.aws_official_description: Amazon Athena is an interactive query service to analyze data directly in Amazon S3 using standard SQL. Athena is serverless, with no infrastructure to set up or manage.
verified_claims: Athena is serverless. You pay only for the queries you run.
Athena scales automatically and runs queries in parallel.
Athena also runs Apache Spark applications without provisioning resources.

core_services.name: Amazon EMR
core_services.job: Managed cluster platform for Apache Hadoop, Spark, and other open-source frameworks.
core_services.choose_when: Spark, Hive, or Hadoop jobs on raw data, with cluster control.
core_services.avoid_when: Plain SQL on S3 (Athena) or ETL with no clusters (Glue).
core_services.trap_words: simple SQL queries, ad-hoc analysis, zero cluster administration
core_services.aws_official_description: Amazon EMR, previously called Amazon Elastic MapReduce, is a managed cluster platform that simplifies running big data frameworks such as Apache Hadoop and Apache Spark on AWS.
verified_claims: EMR was previously named Amazon Elastic MapReduce.
EMR moves large data volumes into and out of Amazon S3 and Amazon DynamoDB.

core_services.name: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
core_services.job: Collects large streams of records in real time for your own consumer applications.
core_services.choose_when: Clickstream, log, or IoT ingest processed by your own consumers. Multiple apps read the same stream.
core_services.avoid_when: You just want data landed in S3 or Redshift with no code. Use Firehose.
core_services.trap_words: automatic delivery, zero administration, no code
core_services.aws_official_description: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams collects and processes large streams of data records in real time. Multiple applications can consume data from the same stream concurrently and independently.
verified_claims: Put-to-get delay is typically under 1 second.
Provisioned mode: each shard supports 1 MB/sec or 1,000 records/sec writes, 2 MB/sec or 2,000 records/sec reads.
Max record payload is 10 MiB. Retention runs from 24 hours to 8,760 hours (365 days).

core_services.name: Amazon Data Firehose
core_services.job: Delivers streaming data to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch, Splunk, Iceberg tables, and HTTP endpoints. No code.
core_services.choose_when: Metrics or logs must land in S3 or Redshift automatically, optionally transformed in flight.
core_services.avoid_when: You need custom stream processing or replay by multiple consumers. Use Kinesis Data Streams.
core_services.trap_words: custom consumer application, sub-second processing, replay the stream
core_services.aws_official_description: Amazon Data Firehose is a fully managed service for delivering real-time streaming data to destinations such as Amazon S3, Amazon Redshift, Amazon OpenSearch Service, Splunk, Apache Iceberg Tables, and custom HTTP endpoints. You do not write applications or manage resources.
verified_claims: Firehose buffers by size (MB) or interval (seconds) before delivery, so it is near real time.
A Firehose record can be as large as 1,000 KB.
Redshift delivery goes to S3 first, then Firehose issues a COPY command.
A Firehose stream can read directly from an existing Kinesis data stream.

core_services.name: AWS Glue
core_services.job: Serverless data integration. Crawlers infer schema into the Data Catalog; jobs run Spark ETL.
core_services.choose_when: Crawl S3 for schema, or convert CSV to Parquet for Athena and Redshift Spectrum.
core_services.avoid_when: You need direct control of a Hadoop or Spark cluster. Use EMR.
core_services.trap_words: managed Hadoop cluster, EC2 cluster tuning
core_services.aws_official_description: AWS Glue is a serverless data integration service to discover, prepare, move, and integrate data from multiple sources. There is no infrastructure to manage.
verified_claims: Glue crawlers infer schema and write it into the AWS Glue Data Catalog.
Cataloged data is queryable from Athena, EMR, and Redshift Spectrum.
Glue supports ETL, ELT, and streaming, including transforming streaming data in transit.

comparisons: EMR vs Glue: EMR is a managed cluster you control. Glue is serverless, built on crawlers, the Data Catalog, and Spark jobs.
Athena vs Redshift: Athena is pay-per-query SQL over S3. Redshift is a columnar warehouse for repeated complex BI queries.
Kinesis Data Streams vs Firehose: Streams is a durable stream your consumers read, retained up to 365 days. Firehose buffers and delivers with no consumer code.
exam_moves: Discover schema from raw S3 into a serverless catalog means Glue crawlers plus Data Catalog.
Load streaming data to S3, Redshift, or OpenSearch with no code means Amazon Data Firehose.
Multiple independent consumers, or replay for days, means Kinesis Data Streams.
Query logs already in S3, immediately, means Athena.

SNS topic fanout to many subscriber endpoints at once.
Application integration (SQS/SNS) vs an email platform (SES).

pub/sub fanout to multiple subscribers
send marketing or transactional email from your domain
strict ordering and no duplicates

core_services.name: Amazon SQS (Simple Queue Service)
core_services.job: Durable hosted queue. Buffers work between producers and consumers so failures do not drop jobs.
core_services.choose_when: Workers cannot keep up with the frontend and jobs must survive until processed.
core_services.avoid_when: One message must reach many subscriber applications. Use SNS, or SNS fanout into SQS queues.
core_services.trap_words: publish/subscribe, multiple subscribers, broadcasting, push notifications
core_services.aws_official_description: Amazon SQS offers a secure, durable, and available hosted queue that lets you integrate and decouple distributed software systems and components. It provides constructs such as dead-letter queues and cost allocation tags.
verified_claims: Default retention is 4 days. Range is 60 seconds to 1,209,600 seconds (14 days).
Max message size is 1,048,576 bytes (1 MiB). Larger payloads go to S3 via the Extended Client Library.
Default visibility timeout is 30 seconds, max 12 hours. A batch request holds at most 10 messages.

core_services.name: Amazon SNS (Simple Notification Service)
core_services.job: Pub/sub topics push one message to many subscribers. Covers A2A and A2P delivery.
core_services.choose_when: One event must hit several targets at once: Lambda, SQS, email, SMS.
core_services.avoid_when: Workers must pull a backlog at their own pace. Use SQS.
core_services.trap_words: pulling messages, buffering a backlog, worker polls the queue
core_services.aws_official_description: Amazon SNS is a fully managed service providing message delivery from publishers to subscribers. Publishers send messages asynchronously to a topic, which is a logical access point and communication channel.
verified_claims: Subscriber endpoints include SQS, Lambda, HTTP(S), email, mobile push, SMS, and Amazon Data Firehose.
SNS supports Application-to-Application (A2A) and Application-to-Person (A2P) messaging.
In fanout, one published message is replicated to multiple endpoints for parallel processing.

core_services.name: Amazon SES (Simple Email Service)
core_services.job: Sends and receives email from your own addresses and domains.
core_services.choose_when: The app sends newsletters, offers, or order confirmations to customers.
core_services.avoid_when: You only need an operational alert or a pub/sub notification. Use SNS.
core_services.trap_words: pub/sub topic, application-to-application messaging, queue buffering
core_services.aws_official_description: Amazon SES is an email platform providing a cost-effective way to send and receive email using your own email addresses and domains.
verified_claims: SES sends marketing email, transactional email such as order confirmations, and newsletters. It also receives mail.
Pricing is based on volume of email sent and received.
SES publishes bounces, complaints, and deliveries to SNS. Received mail can go to S3 or trigger Lambda.

comparisons: SQS vs SNS: SQS is pull-based; consumers poll at their own pace. SNS is push-based; every subscribed endpoint gets the message.
SNS vs SES: SNS sends application notifications and A2P messages. SES is a full email platform for your own domains.
Standard vs FIFO: Standard is at-least-once with duplicates possible and near-unlimited throughput. FIFO gives exactly-once processing and ordering within a message group.
exam_moves: Frontend overwhelmed by processing tasks: put jobs in SQS, let an Auto Scaling group of workers poll it.
One upload must start several independent pipelines: SNS topic fanning out to SQS queues or Lambda functions.
Standard queues are at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent.
Retention is 60 seconds to 14 days, default 4 days. Payloads over 1 MiB must be offloaded to S3.

what_this_tests: Routing AWS, custom, and SaaS events to targets with EventBridge.
Scheduling tasks with cron and rate expressions.
Orchestrating multi-step workflows with retries, catch, parallelism, and human approval.

signal_words.phrase: trigger Lambda when an AWS resource changes state
multi-step workflow with retries and error handling
run a task on a cron or rate schedule

core_services.name: Amazon EventBridge
core_services.job: Serverless event bus. Ingests, filters, transforms, and delivers events to targets by rule.
core_services.choose_when: A resource state change must invoke a target, or a task must run on a schedule.
core_services.avoid_when: You need a pollable backlog (SQS) or stateful multi-step orchestration (Step Functions).
core_services.trap_words: worker queue backlog, buffering, long-running stateful workflow
core_services.aws_official_description: EventBridge is a serverless service that uses events to connect application components. It ingests, filters, transforms, and delivers events.
verified_claims: EventBridge delivers events two ways: event buses (many sources to many targets) and Pipes (point-to-point).
EventBridge Scheduler supports cron and rate expressions plus one-time invocations.
Schedules use UTC+0. Minimum precision is one minute; there is no second-level precision.

core_services.name: AWS Step Functions
core_services.job: Runs state machines that sequence AWS services, with retries, catch, waits, parallel, and map states.
core_services.choose_when: A process needs ordered steps, error handling, branching, or a human approval.
core_services.avoid_when: One event just invokes one target with no state. Use EventBridge.
core_services.trap_words: single-action trigger, simple event routing
core_services.aws_official_description: AWS Step Functions creates workflows, also called state machines, to build distributed applications, automate processes, and orchestrate microservices. The console visualizes, edits, and debugs the workflow.
verified_claims: Standard workflows are exactly-once and run up to one year. Express workflows are at-least-once and run up to five minutes.
Retry and Catch handle errors. Parallel runs branches concurrently; Map iterates over a dataset.
Human approval uses the wait-for-callback (.waitForTaskToken) integration pattern.

core_services.name: Amazon SWF (Simple Workflow Service)
core_services.job: Older workflow service. Coordinates tasks across workers you implement and run yourself.
core_services.choose_when: Legacy SWF workers already exist, or the question names SWF directly.
core_services.avoid_when: Building anything new. AWS recommends Step Functions for most orchestration.
core_services.trap_words: new serverless workflow, visual Workflow Studio, modern orchestration
core_services.aws_official_description: Amazon SWF builds, runs, and scales background jobs with parallel or sequential steps. It coordinates work across distributed components and tracks task state.
verified_claims: AWS states: 'For most use cases, we recommend considering AWS Step Functions for your workflow and orchestration needs.'
SWF workers run on EC2 or on your own premises.

comparisons: EventBridge vs Step Functions: EventBridge routes and schedules. Step Functions holds state across steps and handles retries, catch, parallelism, and approvals.
Step Functions vs SWF: AWS recommends Step Functions for most orchestration. SWF makes you build and run the workers.
Standard vs Express workflows: Standard is exactly-once, up to one year, full history. Express is at-least-once, up to five minutes, for high event rates.
exam_moves: Daily 2 AM Lambda backup means an EventBridge cron schedule. Schedules are UTC, one-minute resolution.
Several Lambdas in sequence with retry and error handling means Step Functions.
Human approval in a workflow is Step Functions with a task token, not SWF.
Hours-to-a-year orchestration means Standard workflows. High-volume, short-lived means Express.

what_this_tests: Picking among backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, and multi-site active/active against RTO and RPO.
Failover and latency routing with Route 53 health checks.
Resilient building blocks: AMIs, ELB, RDS Multi-AZ, S3 durability.

signal_words.phrase: route users to the Region with lowest latency
active-passive failover to a standby Region
signal_words.points_to: Route 53 failover routing with health checks

signal_words.phrase: scaled down but fully functional copy always running
data replicated, servers switched off until failover

core_services.name: Amazon Route 53
core_services.job: DNS service doing three things: domain registration, DNS routing, and health checking.
core_services.choose_when: You need cross-Region failover or latency routing driven by health checks.
core_services.avoid_when: Caching content at the edge (CloudFront) or balancing inside a Region (ELB).
core_services.trap_words: content caching, Layer 7 request routing, edge caching
core_services.aws_official_description: Amazon Route 53 is a highly available and scalable DNS web service. It performs three main functions in any combination: domain registration, DNS routing, and health checking.
verified_claims: Routing policies are simple, failover, geolocation, geoproximity, latency, IP-based, multivalue answer, and weighted.
Failover routing configures active-passive failover.
Latency routing picks the Region giving that user the lowest latency, based on AWS latency data.
Multivalue answer routing returns up to eight healthy records chosen at random.

core_services.name: Multi-Region setups
core_services.job: Places recovery or active workload capacity in more than one Region to survive Regional impairment.
core_services.choose_when: The scenario calls for Regional disaster recovery, active-active routing, warm standby, pilot light, or strict RTO/RPO targets.
core_services.avoid_when: The requirement is only instance, Availability Zone, or maintenance resilience inside one Region. Use Multi-AZ first.
core_services.trap_words: regional outage, active-active, warm standby, pilot light, backup and restore, RTO, RPO
core_services.aws_official_description: Disaster recovery strategies on AWS include backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, and multi-site active-active patterns.
verified_claims: Backup and restore is usually lowest cost and has higher RTO/RPO than standby or active-active designs.
Pilot light keeps core infrastructure replicated while most resources are started during recovery.
Warm standby and multi-site active-active keep more capacity running in the recovery Region for faster recovery.

core_services.name: Amazon EC2 AMIs (Amazon Machine Images)
core_services.job: An image supplying the software to boot an EC2 instance, plus a block device mapping.
core_services.choose_when: Launching identical pre-configured instances, including golden AMIs copied to a DR Region.
core_services.avoid_when: Packaging container images (ECR) or serverless functions.
core_services.trap_words: manual OS configuration after boot, container image
core_services.aws_official_description: An Amazon Machine Image (AMI) provides the software required to set up and boot an EC2 instance. Each AMI contains a block device mapping specifying the block devices to attach.
verified_claims: An AMI is specific to a Region, OS, processor architecture, root volume type, and virtualization type. It can be copied across Regions.
The AWS DR whitepaper recommends backing up EC2 instances as AMIs and copying golden AMIs to primary and backup Regions.

core_services.name: Elastic Load Balancing (ELB)
core_services.job: Distributes traffic across targets in one or more AZs. Routes only to healthy targets.
core_services.choose_when: Spreading requests across a fleet in multiple AZs so one instance or AZ loss is survivable.
core_services.avoid_when: Routing between Regions or by user geography. Use Route 53 or Global Accelerator.
core_services.trap_words: cross-Region routing, DNS resolution, geolocation
core_services.aws_official_description: Elastic Load Balancing automatically distributes incoming traffic across multiple targets, such as EC2 instances, containers, and IP addresses, in one or more Availability Zones. It monitors target health and routes only to healthy targets.
verified_claims: Current generation types are Application, Network, and Gateway Load Balancers. Classic is previous generation; AWS recommends migrating.
The Application Load Balancer operates at layer 7 of the OSI model and routes on path, host, headers, methods, query strings, and source IP.
Auto Scaling registers launched instances with the load balancer and deregisters terminated ones.

core_services.name: Amazon RDS
core_services.job: Managed relational database. AWS handles backups, patching, failure detection, and recovery.
core_services.choose_when: Managed SQL with automated backups, Multi-AZ for HA, or cross-Region read replicas for DR.
core_services.avoid_when: You need OS-level access (EC2) or extreme key-value scaling (DynamoDB).
core_services.trap_words: NoSQL, OS-level access, custom database binaries
core_services.aws_official_description: Amazon RDS is a web service that makes it easier to set up, operate, and scale a relational database in the AWS Cloud. It provides resizable capacity and manages common database administration tasks.
verified_claims: Supported engines: IBM Db2, MariaDB, Microsoft SQL Server, MySQL, Oracle Database, PostgreSQL.
A Multi-AZ DB instance keeps a synchronous standby in another AZ. That standby does not serve reads.
A Multi-AZ DB cluster has one writer and two readers across three AZs; all three serve reads.
Promoting a non-Aurora read replica takes a few minutes and includes a reboot.

core_services.name: Amazon S3
core_services.job: Object storage for backups, data lakes, and static content.
core_services.choose_when: Durable storage for backups and media. Cross-Region Replication copies objects to a DR bucket.
core_services.avoid_when: Low-latency block storage attached to an instance. Use EBS.
core_services.trap_words: block storage, boot volume, file system mount
core_services.aws_official_description: Amazon S3 is an object storage service offering industry-leading scalability, data availability, security, and performance.
verified_claims: S3 Standard is designed for 99.999999999% durability and 99.99% availability across three or more AZs.
S3 One Zone-IA and S3 Express One Zone store data in one AZ and are not resilient to AZ loss.
S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for PUT and DELETE in all Regions.

comparisons: Latency vs geolocation routing: latency picks the Region with the lowest measured latency for that user. Geolocation routes by user location, regardless of speed.

Backup and restore vs pilot light: backup and restore redeploys infrastructure, config, and code at failover. Pilot light keeps data replicated and core infrastructure always provisioned, servers switched off.
Pilot light vs warm standby: AWS states pilot light cannot process requests without further action. Warm standby handles traffic immediately at reduced capacity and only needs scaling up.

Warm standby vs multi-site active/active: active/active serves traffic from every Region and has no failover event. It is the most complex and costly option. Hot standby deploys the same but serves from one Region.
exam_moves: Primary Region fails over to a secondary Region: Route 53 failover routing plus health checks. AWS calls this active-passive.
Cheapest with the worst RTO/RPO is backup and restore. Near-zero RTO at highest cost is multi-site active/active.
AWS says use data plane operations at failover, such as Route 53 health checks, not control plane operations like weight changes or Auto Scaling.
AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS) implements the pilot light strategy using a staging VPC.

what_this_tests: Analyze past spend (Cost Explorer) vs alert and act on thresholds (Budgets).
Multi-account governance with Organizations, SCPs, and Control Tower.
Savings Plans commitments and consolidated billing discounts.

signal_words.phrase: visualize and analyze past cost and usage trends
alert me before I exceed a spending threshold
central guardrails across many AWS accounts
signal_words.points_to: AWS Organizations SCPs / AWS Control Tower

signal_words.phrase: commit to $/hour of compute for 1 or 3 years

core_services.name: AWS Cost Explorer
core_services.job: Views and analyzes cost and usage over time. Charts, cost and usage reports, RI reports, forecasts.
core_services.choose_when: Finding which service, account, or tag drove a bill spike.
core_services.avoid_when: You want threshold alerts or automated actions. Use Budgets.
core_services.trap_words: hard spending limit, automatically stop resources, real-time alert
core_services.aws_official_description: AWS Cost Explorer is a tool that enables you to view and analyze your costs and usage, using the main graph, cost and usage reports, or RI reports.
verified_claims: Cost Explorer shows up to 13 months of history, the current month, and 18 months of forecast.
Data refreshes at least every 24 hours. The UI is free; each paginated API request costs $0.01.
Cost Explorer provides Reserved Instance purchase recommendations.

core_services.name: AWS Budgets
core_services.job: Tracks cost and usage against thresholds. Alerts by email or SNS, and can trigger budget actions.
core_services.choose_when: Alert before monthly spend crosses a threshold, or monitor RI and Savings Plans utilization.
core_services.avoid_when: Deep historical trend analysis. Use Cost Explorer.
core_services.trap_words: historical analysis, visualizing past usage, RI purchase recommendations
core_services.aws_official_description: AWS Budgets lets you track and take action on your AWS costs and usage, and monitor utilization and coverage metrics for Reserved Instances or Savings Plans.
verified_claims: Budget types: cost, usage, RI utilization, RI coverage, Savings Plans utilization, Savings Plans coverage.
Alerts fire on actual or forecasted amounts, delivered to email, an SNS topic, or both.
Budget actions can apply a control, such as a custom IAM policy denying new resource provisioning.
Budgets data updates up to three times a day, typically 8-12 hours apart.

core_services.name: AWS Organizations
core_services.job: Creates and groups accounts into OUs, applies policies such as SCPs, and consolidates billing.
core_services.choose_when: Many accounts need one bill plus central permission guardrails.
core_services.avoid_when: Per-user permissions (IAM) or VPC connectivity (Transit Gateway, peering).
core_services.trap_words: IAM user permissions, VPC routing, network connectivity
core_services.aws_official_description: AWS Organizations helps you centrally manage and govern your environment as you scale. You create accounts, group them, apply policies for governance, and simplify billing with a single payment method.
verified_claims: SCPs control access to AWS resources, services, and Regions across the organization. RCPs prevent unintended resource use.
Accounts group into organizational units (OUs). Organizations provides a single consolidated bill.
Organizations integrates with Control Tower, CloudTrail, Config, Backup, and RAM.

core_services.name: AWS Control Tower
core_services.job: Builds and governs a multi-account landing zone. Orchestrates Organizations, Service Catalog, and IAM Identity Center.
core_services.choose_when: Standing up a governed multi-account environment with controls and standardized account provisioning.
core_services.avoid_when: You only need billing rules or cost reports on an existing organization.
core_services.trap_words: single-account setup, granular custom billing rule, cost analysis
core_services.aws_official_description: AWS Control Tower sets up and governs an AWS multi-account environment following prescriptive best practices. It orchestrates AWS Organizations, AWS Service Catalog, and AWS IAM Identity Center to build a landing zone in less than an hour.
verified_claims: A landing zone is a multi-account environment built on security and compliance best practices, created in under an hour.
Controls (guardrails) are preventive, detective, or proactive, and are mandatory, strongly recommended, or elective.
Account Factory is a configurable template standardizing new account provisioning.
Control Tower detects drift, meaning divergence from best practices.

core_services.name: Compute Savings Plans
core_services.job: Discounts compute in exchange for a $/hour commitment over one or three years.
core_services.choose_when: Steady baseline spend across EC2, Fargate, and Lambda, without locking to an instance family.
core_services.avoid_when: Unpredictable workloads with no committable baseline, or database discounts (use RDS RIs).
core_services.trap_words: locked to a specific instance family (that is EC2 Instance Savings Plans or EC2 RIs), database discounts
core_services.aws_official_description: Savings Plans provide savings beyond On-Demand rates in exchange for a commitment to a specified amount of compute power, measured per hour, for a one or three year period. Compute Savings Plans lower EC2 prices regardless of instance family, size, OS, tenancy, or Region, and also cover Fargate and Lambda.
verified_claims: AWS states savings of up to 72% on compute workloads.
Compute Savings Plans apply regardless of instance family, size, OS, tenancy, or Region, and cover Fargate and Lambda.
Terms are one year (365 days) or three years (1,095 days), with All upfront, Partial upfront, or No upfront payment.
SageMaker AI Savings Plans cover SageMaker AI instance usage.

core_services.name: Consolidated billing (AWS Organizations)
core_services.job: One bill for all accounts. Combines usage so accounts share volume, RI, and Savings Plans discounts.
core_services.choose_when: Multiple accounts should pool usage to reach cheaper pricing tiers.
core_services.avoid_when: You need a security boundary. Billing is not access control; use SCPs and IAM.
core_services.trap_words: security boundary, IAM permissions, isolation of access
core_services.aws_official_description: Consolidated billing in AWS Organizations consolidates billing and payment for multiple AWS accounts. The management account pays the charges of all member accounts.
verified_claims: Combined usage shares volume pricing discounts, Reserved Instance discounts, and Savings Plans.
Consolidated billing costs nothing extra.
Member account bills are informational only.

comparisons: Cost Explorer vs Budgets: Cost Explorer analyzes 13 months back and forecasts 18 months forward. Budgets alerts or acts when actual or forecast crosses a threshold.

Organizations vs Control Tower: Organizations supplies accounts, OUs, policies, and consolidated billing. Control Tower orchestrates it into a landing zone with controls, Account Factory, and drift detection.

Compute Savings Plans vs EC2 Instance Savings Plans vs RIs: Compute plans are the most flexible, covering any family, size, OS, tenancy, Region, plus Fargate and Lambda. The others trade flexibility for a deeper discount on one family in one Region.
Multi-AZ vs multi-Region: RDS Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby in another AZ in the same Region. Multi-Region designs protect against losing an entire Region.
exam_moves: Notify me before I exceed a dollar amount means AWS Budgets. Explain last month's bill means Cost Explorer.
Block a service or Region across every member account means an SCP in AWS Organizations.
New governed multi-account environment with guardrails means AWS Control Tower.
For highest web-tier availability, span an Auto Scaling group across at least two AZs behind an ELB.
A rack-level spread placement group allows at most seven running instances per AZ per group.
Consolidated billing pools discounts but is not a security boundary.
